analysis.one_liner: Creates universal basic health insurance funded by cigarette taxes and a payroll tax on employers who don't offer coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after introduction in May 1989 with 3 cosponsors, it sat in two House subcommittees until that Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new public program, 'Basic Health Insurance,' that every U.S. citizen and lawful resident could join. The government would set minimum benefits, sign up private insurance carriers through competitive bidding, and charge enrollees premiums that rise with their income and wealth. To pay for it, cigarette taxes would go up and employers who did not offer a health plan meeting the new standards would pay a tax equal to 6% of their total wages.
analysis.who_benefits: People with no health coverage, people denied coverage for preexisting conditions, and lower-income households, who would gain access to a basic health plan they could always enroll in, with premiums scaled to what they can pay. The bill expressly bars carriers from turning anyone down or restricting coverage because of a preexisting condition or previous treatment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. national and lawfully admitted alien would be eligible to enroll with a participating carrier, with no evidence of medical insurability required.
Coverage could not be restricted because of a preexisting condition or previous treatment.
Benefit standards would include maternity, prenatal, and postnatal care and catastrophic protection, set at the group-policy level so families are covered together.
Premiums would be set by a formula tied to income and net assets, so they rise with wealth, and enrollees who make little use of the insurance would get a discount.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, through a new additional federal excise tax on cigarettes on top of existing taxes; and employers who do not offer their employees a health plan meeting the bill's benefit standards, who would pay an excise tax of 6% of total wages paid. Any shortfall beyond the cigarette-tax revenue would come from general Treasury funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Smokers and employers without health plans

drawbacks.text: The program's dedicated funding is 100% of the cigarette excise tax, a tax that falls hardest on lower-income smokers and that shrinks over time as smoking declines, leaving general taxpayer funds to cover the gap.
Employers who do not offer a qualifying plan would owe a tax of 6% of total wages, a cost that could fall back on workers through lower pay or hiring.

The new coverage would be secondary to any other insurance or benefit plan, meaning it pays only after existing coverage, a complicated layering that could limit its practical value for people who already have partial coverage.

The program would deliver a public entitlement entirely through private insurance carriers chosen by competitive bidding, locking those carriers in as the permanent channel for basic coverage rather than creating a government-run plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large: guaranteed, portable basic coverage for everyone, including people insurers could otherwise turn away, financed in part by a tax on a harmful product. The costs are real: a regressive cigarette tax that erodes over time, a 6%-of-wages tax on uncovered employers, and a design that routes public money through private carriers under government-set rates, which could either restrain premiums or simply entrench the industry as middleman. The bill was never debated in public, so none of these tradeoffs were ever tested in Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, then to their health subcommittees, and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald J. Pease introduced the bill on May 3, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
On May 10 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and on May 22 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the last action of any kind was the May 22, 1989 subcommittee referral.
The bill drew only 3 cosponsors, all House Democrats, out of 257 Democrats in the chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the pre-1990 status quo held: employers without health plans avoided a new 6%-of-wages tax, smokers avoided a higher excise tax, and private health insurers faced no new government-run contracting system. The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, smokers, and insurers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, and its only recorded support was its Democratic sponsor plus 3 of 257 House Democrats as cosponsors, with no Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have made private carriers the permanent delivery channel for universal basic coverage: the Secretary would contract with carriers chosen by competitive bidding and pay them from federal funds, giving the industry a guaranteed enrollee pool, but under government-set benefit standards and bid rates. It regulates the industry at the same time it locks in its central role.

The bill imposes an additional federal excise tax on cigarettes (higher rates for large cigars and for tobacco weighing over 3 pounds per thousand), which raises prices and reduces sales. Because the bill died, the industry avoided the increase.
Employers not offering a plan meeting the bill's benefit standards would owe an excise tax of 6% of total wages, giving them a direct financial stake in the bill's failure.
